dedupe_keys.name: united states effects of 32 rural hospital closures on acute and post acute care

description: This case study measures what happened to hospital and post-acute care use and outcomes for older adults after rural hospitals closed. The authors, researchers at the University of Michigan and Syracuse University, used a staggered difference-in-differences design on 32 rural hospital closures, with 100 percent Medicare claims and home health and skilled nursing facility clinical data covering about 3 million discharges, and published the work in an open-access journal article. Outcomes at county level include travel distance, length of stay, functional limits at the start of post-acute care, readmissions, mortality, fall injuries and population hospitalisation and death rates. Coverage is rural counties across the United States. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence; Medicare data need a data use agreement. Caveats: the analysis covers fee-for-service Medicare only and closures are not random. Closing hospitals served more minoritised, lower-income and Medicaid patients and had lower margins. After closure, quarterly hospitalisation rates rose by 111.6 per 10,000 older adults and stays lengthened by 0.34 days, but travel distance, function and time to post-acute care did not change; readmissions rose slightly where hospitals were isolated. Simulation uses: effect sizes for facility loss scenarios in healthcare access and resilience models. Related records: the surgical study of rural closures (case_study-us-rural-hospital-closures-surgical-quality-access) looks at surgery.
